Q1780180.summary: Christ stands upon the cross alive, eyes open and head gently inclined, robed like a king in a long belted tunic that leaves only his hands and feet bare — the Lord who reigns from the tree. Medieval pilgrims believed Nicodemus, who helped bury Jesus, had carved it and that an angel finished the face; it became one of the most venerated images of Christ in Europe, copied from England to Catalonia. In 2020 radiocarbon dating placed the wood in the late 8th or early 9th century, revealing it to be one of the oldest wooden crucifixes of the Christian West.
facts: Until the 2020 results, many scholars believed the present crucifix was a 12th- or 13th-century replacement of a lost original.
The legend tells that the image came from the Holy Land in a boat with no sail or crew, and was brought to Lucca on an ox-cart without a driver in 782.
It stands in a marble tempietto built for it by Matteo Civitali in 1484; every 13 September the city honours it with the candlelit Luminara procession.
King William II of England is said to have sworn 'by the Holy Face of Lucca'.
Q1780180.notes: Radiocarbon range reported as 770–880 on en.wikipedia and as late 8th–early 9th century on it.wikipedia; the Commons photographer labels it 780–820. The crucifix was re-presented on 13 September 2025 after restoration in a space in the left aisle while its tempietto is restored. Supersedes the WGA record wga:m/master/xunk_it/xunk_it6/03cross (wrongly dated c. 1200), rejected in deep-c1-legends.json.

cur:monumental-san-raising-of-lazarus.summary: Lazarus, still wrapped in his grave-clothes, stands in the doorway of a small temple-like tomb at the top of a flight of steps, as Christ, haloed and in purple, stretches out his hand to call him forth, a disciple at his side. Unlike the catacomb paintings, Christ here commands with a gesture rather than a wand.
facts: The thirteen scenes of the north wall show Christ's miracles and teaching; in all of them he appears young and beardless, robed in imperial purple.
The Raising of Lazarus, read near the end of Lent before Holy Week, was one of the most frequently depicted miracles in Early Christian art.
The scenes were not arranged in biblical order but are thought to follow the Gospel readings of the Lenten liturgy in Theodoric's palace church.

feat:facundus-beatus-throne-vision.summary: Framed in an arched opening and flanked by two great angels, the One seated on the throne appears at the top of the page, while below, within a great starry circle, the Lamb of God stands at the centre, surrounded by the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders with their harps, with further angels at its edges. In flat, blazing colours, the Iberian painters turned Saint John's vision into a vibrant, almost abstract pattern. The image presents Christ as the slain Lamb who alone is worthy to open the book of history.
facts: The manuscript was made for King Ferdinand I of León and Queen Sancha, and is one of the richest of the illustrated copies of Beatus of Liébana's eighth-century Commentary on the Apocalypse.
The scribe Facundus names himself in the colophon, and the book is dated 1047; the name of its painter is not recorded.
It contains 98 miniatures, whose saturated colour bands derive from the Mozarabic tradition of Christian Spain.
Beatus manuscripts are often seen as reflecting an urgent apocalyptic reading of history among Christians living on the frontier with al-Andalus.
